REQUEST FOR ACTION TO CONTROL VIOLENCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since it has become urgent to control violence in sports generally and particularly in hockey; since violent fights, blows and excessive brutality are not at the present time covered under criminal law; and, finally, since control over sports activities is generally left to the goodwill of sports monopolies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House direct the government to take all necessary arrangements in the shortest time possible so as to use any legal mechanism to punish rightly acts of violence in sports generally, particularly in hockey, and so as to develop amateur sports and invite people to play an active part.

Comparing Unemployment Statistics with Data from the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
The monthly Labour Force Survey (LFS) is the source of the official measure of unemployment in Canada. Comparisons are frequently made between the number of unemployed persons as reported by the LFS and the number of unemployment insurance claimants or beneficiaries. The numbers in the series seldom coincide, and misleading inferences are often drawn about the accuracy of the measures. However, the series are not intended to measure the same characteristics or identical populations and therefore, direct comparisons are not valid. The populations to which the LFS and Unemployment Insurance Commission (UIC) data refer are somewhat different in several respects. The Labour Force Survey covers the civilian population 14 years of age and over, including selfemployed persons but excluding the institutional population and persons living in the Yukon, Northwest Territories and Indian reserves. The insured population comprises the paid worker segment of the labour force (1), including members of the armed forces. Further problems in comparing the LFS unemployed and the UIC claimants and beneficiaries result from the fact that there are significant differences in the meaning of the terms "unemployed", "claimant" and "beneficiary". Not all the LFS unemployed are UIC claimants (beneficiaries) and conversely, not all UIC claimants (beneficiaries) are included in the LFS unemployed. According to LFS definitions, some UIC claimants may be "employed", while others may be "not in the Labour force". The LFS unemployment estimates

April 29, 1976

include primarily, persons who were without work and seeking work. To be entitled to receive UIC benefit, a claimant must have had an interruption of earnings, and be available for and capable of employment. A UIC claimant may work part-time and still be eligible for benefit while in the LFS such a person would be considered as employed. Although a claimant may meet the condition of availability and capability, he may not be actively seeking employment and, therefore, would be treated by the LFS as not in the Labour force. Thus, in addition to persons who would be classified as unemployed according to the LFS, the UIC claimant count includes persons with some earnings (employed) as well as persons not actively seeking employment (not in the labour force). For example, most claimants eligible for UIC sickness, maternity and retirement benefit are probably not included in the LFS unemployed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for the annoncement about his busy schedule. I think an answer to the question asked today in the House is of great pertinence, particularly to the Atlantic area. The target for the reduction of the inflationary rate in Canada is much lower than the target and the anticipated rate of reduction of inflation in the United States. I suppose no area of Canada is more affected by such a situation than the Atlantic area. Our dealings, to a very large degree, depend not only upon the success of the economy of Canada as a whole, but upon our competitive position in relation to producers in the markets of the world and in the United States. Every time the economy of Canada is not in pace with that of the United States, the Atlantic area suffers much more than the rest of Canada.
Whether it be in respect of wood products, agricultural or any other products, we are constantly in competition either in United States markets or world markets with products produced there. If, for instance, one is involved in the paper industry, one finds oneself in competition with that industry in the state of Maine and throughout the eastern coast of the United States as far south as Georgia. Every advantage they can obtain from a declining rate of
Anti-Inflation Act
inflation is detrimental to our forestry and agricultural industries, at least in the Atlantic area. It is, therefore, the plea of that area that the government improve its target. The government must reduce the time-span required to reduce the inflationary structure and prevent the undue hardship which would fall on the Atlantic area.
If they, per chance-and I hope they do-reach the 2 per cent rate in the target time mentioned today in the United States, this certainly will place an undue cost on the Atlantic area. I think this is particularly pertinent in view of the fact that Anti-Inflation Board rulings already have decreed that workers in the Atlantic area are not entitled to wages equivalent to those of workers in other parts of Canada. Two instances have been cited. The first is in respect of the pulp and paper industry in the city of Saint John, which had been closing the gap but had not completely closed it in respect of the wages received by comparable industry in central Canada and on the British Columbia coast. They were also not allowed by the board to attain the wage level paid in the sugar industry.
It has been extremely difficult for this particular industry to obtain help at the rates of pay that have been paid. While the industry had tried, in the negotiations with its workers, to apply a rate which would provide stability with regard to the work force, this was rolled back by the Anti-Inflation Board. When one couples this with the policy of the government of Canada concerning regional wages in different parts of Canada, and when the same wages under certain agreements between the government of Canada and the unions are not paid in the Atlantic area, there is a discriminatory structure which does no good to the Atlantic area on an economic basis.
The basic structure, of course, requires co-operation among the government, management, and all other facets of our society. This is an aspect which has been lacking while the government has been trying to administer this bill. Therefore, the quicker the government gets out of its present posture in respect of price and wage controls, the better it will be for the amenities of the various groups in Canada, and the better it will be for Canada as a whole.
We cannot conduct ourselves on the basis of confrontation with labour. We cannot conduct ourselves on the basis of confrontation with industry. We cannot conduct ourselves on the basis of confrontation with the provinces. We must change the pattern and talk about the things this government intends to do, so that there will be some accord when the government comes up with a final policy.
Like so many other pieces of legislation, this bill was not presented to parliament by a government which had had proper discussion with all the other forces in Canada or which had properly explained the legislation, or its necessity, to the people of Canada at any stage and explained to the manufacturer and the labourer the real need and necessity for such a program. Instead, there has been confrontation.
The government of Canada suggested it borrowed this policy from the opposition. Mr. Speaker, it must be made abundantly clear, in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in answer to a question today, that although he may have borrowed the semblance of a policy, obviously he did not borrow the policy of the opposition. While there may be an element of relationship between the anti-infla-

April 29, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
tion legislation we have on the statute books and what the opposition would have brought in, it is not the policy of the opposition which has been brought in.
I believe the time has come when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) should not confront and challenge the people. Government speakers, as they go back and forth across the country, should not tell the people what to do. Instead, they should show leadership by giving information and by answering questions in this House. They should give forthright and full information to the voters across Canada concerning the implications and complications of our economic structure. If this were done, the amendment presently before us should be accepted, because it would not take more than 2Vi years to bring about the changes that are required in our economy.
The Canadian people in Saint John and other areas of Canada should not be kicked around as they are by this government. Canadians are good people. They can, and will, take good advice. They will follow when they are well led, but they cannot accept confrontation as we have it. This legislation is directly responsible for the approach taken by labour, whether it be at the level of the school teacher or of the janitor, not because these people are not prepared to make their contribution to our society but because they have been confronted. This is what is wrong. This is why the adoption of this amendment would be good for the government, would be good for the opposition and would be good for the whole of Canada.
Legislation has continually hurt the Atlantic area. Whether it be in respect of transportation, fishing or agriculture, it would seem that the policies of this government, through Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance, have been to look at dollars and how to save them, but not to look at the consequences of saving money in particular fields. This is but another example of the inequities and inequalities which have existed and which will continue to exist in the Atlantic area until we have a total policy presented by the government of Canada to bring the whole of Canada ahead at once without neglecting any part of Canada.
This piece of legislation gives no consideration to the exceptions which invariably will be necessary in one part of Canada or another. This legislation does improve the basic principle of the Anti-Inflation Board; there is no question about that. Without the recognition by government of exceptions, without the recognition by government of the requirements in certain specific areas, without a cost-benefit study of the impact of legislation upon certain areas of Canada, this country cannot go forward as a country but will only go forward in those parts in which the government is particularly interested and apparently in which it holds most of its seats.
I appeal to the government to accept this amendment. Let us not confront the people; let us publicly consult them. There was a reference by the Prime Minister today to consultation, but there was no indication that the nation would have any idea of the type of consultation that would take place. There was no indication that the public would ever know what was said in the private and secretive type

of consultations which he implied would take place. This is not the way in which a government should govern. It should be for what is right and fair in its policies.
I ask that when this legislation passes, as it will, unquestionably, with the weight of the government, that the minister give careful consideration-as he directs those controlling the anti-inflation program-to the impact of the individual agreement upon an individual area before he lowers the boom and says "No." Let us try to create an element of equality of earning opportunity across this nation. Let us not deny those in the east the privileges which are enjoyed in the extreme west, the prairies and the centre of Canada. We do not need to be treated as exceptions-we just want to be treated as Canadians!

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for a few minutes in response to some remarks that were made yesterday. I want to remind the House that this bill is before parliament because the NDP, both at the time of the passage of the original legislation and as a result of Standing Order 26 in a special debate, insisted on the necessity for legislation to provide for appeal procedures for workers and salary earners in Canada against decisions made under the anti-inflation program.
I noticed yesterday that none of the members of the official opposition mentioned that that happens to be the main purpose of the bill, that is, to provide some justice and fair play to workers in Canada. They spent a great deal of time weeping and wailing for insurance companies, corporations, etc., but they forgot to mention the main purport of the bill, that is, to establish an appeal procedure for wage and salary earners in Canada, many of whom have already been unjustly treated as a result of the decision of the AIB and the administrator.
Yesterday, a spokesman of the official opposition stated that these kinds of controls should have limitations, that they should expire next year. The amendment reads, "May 1, 1977". They tore the program to shreds and, as my leader said earlier in the debate, they damned the progress from stem to gudgeon, then moved an amendment to keep it going for another year. I have not yet seen any proper reconciliation of that kind of nonsense.

The issue is not how long the controls should be in place. Surely the issue is what kind of controls there should be, to whom they should apply, and how people will be affected by them. If the controls had started with those on high incomes, those who make high profits, those who have incomes from high interest rates, and if they had begun at the top and worked downward, whether it be incomes from profits, interest rates, investments or wages and salaries, then surely that would have been some kind of justice and equity in a program to fight inflation.
I heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) complain yesterday about the "poor" banks, insurance and finance companies that will be brought under the control program. He shed tears for them. Surely that is precisely where the program should have started, with banks, insurance and finance companies. Surely they should have been the first to come under a program to
April 29, 1976

fight inflation. One of the spokesmen of the official opposition cries for the "poor" banks, insurance and finance companies, but I did not hear a word from the official opposition yesterday about any guarantees that old age pensioners should get what is allowed as a minimum under the anti-inflation program, that is, $600 a year. I would have hoped the official opposition would have taken action to impress upon this government the importance of bringing in immediately a $50 a month increase for old age pensioners.
People on low wages and salaries and people on pensions are not the ones who cause inflation; they are the first victims of inflation. But the whole program attacks these people first. The hon. member for Edmonton West worries about what will happen to the banks, insurance and finance companies when they are brought under the controls. That is the evidence the people of Canada have as to where the Conservative party stands when it comes to fighting inflation. They will look after their friends, the rich and the "barefoot" boys from Bay Street and James Street. They talk a good fight about workers, but when it comes to the crunch, when it comes to proposing legislation or moving amendments to legislation, they worry about banks, insurance and finance companies. It is not the people whose wage increases have been rolled back or whose bargaining process has been interfered with who cause inflation. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: UNITED GRAIN GROWERS LIMITED
speechtext:
that Bill S-33, respecting United Grain Growers Limited, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak on second reading of Bill S-33. The bill is not as contentious as the last piece of business the House just voted on, and I dare say it will enjoy the support of all parties and all members of this House.
It was both a pleasure and privilege to move second reading of Bill S-33, an act respecting United Grain Growers Limited, or UGG as they are commonly known across the prairies. It is a well known, well established prairie grain company which was originally set up by producers to buy and market grain. Since its earliest days it has expanded, as have other co-operative grain companies on the prairies, and become involved in the handling of chemicals, feeds and other matters related to the interests of grain producers.

The company was first organized by act of the Manitoba legislature in 1902, and later incorporated by the Senate and the House of Commons in 1911 under the name of Grain Growers Company Limited. The company has a long and illustrious history of service to western grain producers. It is organized on a co-operative basis, involving producers throughout the western grain growing region. Terms which have become widely used in the last few years in the cattle industry-"cross-bred" and "exotic"- apply, I think, to this particular company. It is a co-operative company with a corporate structure. At least, that is how it was to be set up under the original legislation, as I understand it. At present, UGG is led by a group of producer-elected directors under Mr. A. M. Runciman, president. The company has been not only active in doing an excellent job for its own members and shippers, but has performed good service for all producers of the prairie region.
The principles of the bill the House is considering are fairly simple and straightforward. Bills of a similar nature relating to UGG have been introduced in the House of Commons and passed, over the years. The bill requests an increase in the capital structure of the company from the present level of $12 million to $25 million. There shall be issued, altogether, 1.2 million class A shares at $20 each, and 200,000 class B or membership shares with a par value of $5 each. This will increase the capitalization of the company and enable it to perform the tasks it is required to undertake.
The bill also proposes to allow the company to increase the dividend rate on class A shares, which are in essence preferred shares, from the existing limit of 6.5 per cent to a new limit of 8 per cent, which represents an increase of 1.5 per cent in the interest rate paid. It also seeks to increase the number of shares which may be held by an individual from 2,500 to 5,000.1 commend the bill to the House and ask that it be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.

subsubtopic: UNITED GRAIN GROWERS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to place on the record today a few brief comments with respect to Bill S-33. It is a pleasure primarily for two reasons: first, it is a refreshing change whenever this House gives its attention to agricultural legislation-and I regret that these opportunities are all too infrequent-and, second, as a personal comment it pleases me to have an opportunity, as a member from central Canada, to lend my support to a just and deserving cause in some other region of this country, in this case western Canada.
My research indicates that the United Grain Growers was first established and chartered by an act of parliament some 70 years ago, in 1906. My colleague for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) suggested that the company was incorporated by act of the Manitoba legislature. He may well be correct.
The United Grain Growers is a result of the encouragement and foresight of the territorial grain growers association, who with some imagination might be compared to a group similar in nature, namely, the Federation of Agriculture. From a small beginning, under good management and producer participation and support, it has grown and developed with remarkable success. With establishment in
Whittaker
Wise
Woolliams Yewchuk-52.
April 29, 1976

Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, it lists some 475 manager units and operates some 700 grain elevators with terminals in Vancouver and Thunder Bay. It is an agent of the Canadian Wheat Board and, in addition, carries on business transactions in non-board grains, domestic feed grains, farm supplies, feeds and fertilizers. One would be remiss, when talking about the organization, if one did not mention its publication, "Country Guide". This agricultural magazine enjoys excellent readership and distribution throughout the entire country and well beyond our borders.
It is estimated that United Grain Growers handle approximately 16 per cent of the grain grown in western Canada. This bill is not unusual, nor is it unique. In 1941 and in 1965, and perhaps on other occasions, similar bills have been presented with respect to changes deemed necessary and desirable. The bill of 1941 amended the charter of the United Grain Growers to provide for two types of shares. First, it created $20 investment shares to be placed on the exchange, and second it created $5 membership or voting shares, the latter to be held only by members who could be regarded solely as producers or legitimate farmers. This was a desirable amendment because it ensured that this farmer-owned co-operative remained in the hands and under the control of producers. The 1965 amendment enabled the United Grain Growers to pay greater dividend or interest on their shares, up to 5 per cent, with the option of paying an additional 1.5 per cent.
Bill S-33 proposes another suitable revision, if that is allowed: first, an increase in capital from the present $12 million to $25 million; second, the right to increase dividends on some shares by a maximum of 3 per cent, giving a total yield of 8 per cent ; and third, an increase in the number of shares to be held by an individual from 2,500 to 5,000.
The record of this co-operative clearly demonstrates a steady growth and a sound financial position both now and over the years. It is a fine example of a united effort by producers successfully to establish and manage a commercial enterprise. It has served the interests of producers in western Canada over the years and I am confident that with these changes it will continue to do so for generations to come.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate the support of my party for this bill and to further indicate our full support and anxiety for its speedy passage.

subsubtopic: UNITED GRAIN GROWERS LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we agree that this legislation should receive speedy passage in this House, in the other place, and royal assent. However, this is an opportunity to make a few points that are appropriate considering the co-operative with which we are dealing. The history goes back to 1906 and involves some of the patron saints in western agriculture, people like George Mothewell, E. A. Partridge and other old-timers in the co-operative movement of the prairies. Some are still alive and are active members of the United Grain Growers, the various wheat pools and farm unions. Hon. members will agree that they deserve full honour, credit and tribute.
United Grain Growers
Co-operatives came into existence as a result of economic tribulations caused by private enterprisers in the so-called free and open market-the grain speculators. Farmers were forced to ban together into co-operatives and start their own elevator companies. As a result, organizations such as the United Grain Growers have grown and expanded. They are the vehicle by which many thousand grain producers in western Canada market their grain. They know they can have confidence in their organization to work on behalf of their best interests.
As the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mcl-saac) pointed out, the legislation allows the United Grain Growers to increase its capitalization from $12 million to $25 million. Not only the United Grain Growers, but the wheat pools as well, will be faced in coming years with the necessity of further modernizing their country elevator system and enlarging their operations. This will be necessary because the pools and the United Grain Growers handle the overwhelming majority of grains marketed in the three prairie provinces. They will obviously need many millions of dollars for these expanded operations. Both the United Grain Growers and the pools have programs to construct new country elevators which will be more modern and efficient. In addition to doing a better job of cleaning, drying and mixing grain, they will have a larger capacity which will allow them to better utilize unit train systems.
The legislation provides that a producer member may hold up to 5,000 class A shares instead of 250. I am confident the additional capital will be used to expand United Grain Growers in the way in which it presently operates. I am confident that none of the money will be used for something like an inland terminal of the nature and kind being promoted by the multinational and international grain dealers such as Cargill and Continental. I know the board of directors, shareholders and members of United Grain Growers will join with the farmers of western Canada in opposing that kind of development. The capital they raise through this legislation will be used to expand their country elevator system. It will serve their organization in many hundreds of shipping points in the three prairie provinces and the Peace River district of British Columbia.
I hope the United Grain Growers, its members, shareholders and board of directors will begin not only to accept but to welcome its employees becoming part of the trade union movement. I speak in particular of the elevator agents, construction and maintenance crews. I hope the shareholders and the board of directors of the United Grain Growers will not just acquiesce but will encourage their country elevator agents, as well as their maintenance and construction crews, to join the Grain Services Union which now has in its ranks all elevator agents, construction and maintenance employees of the Saskatchewan and Manitoba pool elevators.
I know that some individual members have made inquiries and that there have been some quiet meetings and discussions. I am confident the management of United Grain Growers will not throw up any roadblocks or make any threats that will hinder or impede their employees becoming members of the Grain Services Union.

April 29, 1976
United Grain Growers
In the course of acquiring additional capital from the operations and modernizing their country elevator system, United Grain Growers, as well as the three prairie pools in servicing their members, are running into difficulty because of impediments imposed partly by the federal government and partly by our transportation system. Only today we were informed of a decision by the cabinet which will do a great deal of harm to organizations such as United Grain Growers and will have a direct as well as an indirect interest in not only rapeseed but rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal. The decision by the government came after an appeal by the co-operatives of the three prairie provinces, the Farmers' Union and the three prairie provincial governments to the cabinet against an order by the Canadian Transport Commission to keep freight rates on rapeseed oil and meal at the level at which they were compared to rapeseed.
Even with the rates as they were, 100 pounds of rapeseed crushed in Saskatchewan into 38 pounds of rapeseed oil, and shipped in a jumbo car at the lowest possible rate to Montreal, cost $1.10 a hundredweight. For 62 pounds of meal, made from 100 pounds of crushed rapeseed, it cost 23.5 cents a hundredweight to Thunder Bay or 59 cents a hundredweight to Montreal. However, if that rapeseed were crushed at Montreal, the statutory rates to Thunder Bay of 23.5 cents, and Thunder Bay to Montreal of 44 cents, makes a total of 67.5 cents, compared to a total of 93 cents if the grain is crushed in Saskatchewan. That is the difference. Under the old rates the 25l/2 cents per hundredweight favoured crushing rapeseed in Montreal or any other point east of Georgian Bay. That is a severe handicap for the rapeseed mills and crushing plants of Western Canada.
When United Grain Growers raise this further capital as proposed in the bill, they will be faced with a further handicap. Let me refer to order in council P.C. 1976-894 of April 13, which was passed by this cabinet:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport, pursuant to section 64 of the National Transportation Act, is pleased hereby to vary the following orders and decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission:
(a)	Order No. R-16824 dated June 27,1973;
(b)	Order No. R-17016 dated August 2, 1973; and
(c)	any other order or decision of the Canadian Transport Commission that is inconsistent with paragraph (d) hereof
to provide
(d)	that the following rates or portions of rates for domestic and export movement of rapeseed meal and rapeseed oil from the four rapeseed crushing plants at Altona, Nipawin, Saskatoon and Lethbridge, be established annually at minimum compensatory levels:
(i)	rates for rapeseed meal and rapeseed oil moving west;-
That is to Vancouver.
(ii)	rates for rapeseed oil moving east; and
(iii)	the portions of rates pertaining to the movement of rapeseed
meal east of Thunder Bay or Armstrong, Ontario.
This will mean that the United Grain Growers, Sask Wheat Pool and any other privately owned rapeseed plant in the three prairie provinces will be faced with an even greater differential when it comes to processing rapeseed into rapessed oil or rapeseed meal. I suggest that investment of any of the additional capital that will be raised under this legislation in a rapeseed plant will be difficult

to justify or merely to break even on. That is because they will be faced with what in polite language can be called an historical anomaly but which is really outright, rank discrimination, which western Canadians have been facing in terms of our freight rate structure for many decades. After raising this additional capital, if United Grain Growers want to go into rapeseed crushing they will continue to be treated as hewers of wood and drawers of water, as we in the three prairie provinces always have been.
Historically we have always had difficulty with freight rates in western Canada when it comes to raw and finished products, whether beef or hogs and the processing thereof, or whether processing wheat into flour. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), that great friend of the farmer, has another bill on the order paper, Bill C-87, to remove the freight rate subsidy on flour. Our grain co-operatives in western Canada own a flour mill. In the middle of negotiations with the Russians for the sale of 275,000 tons of flour, they found they could not give the Russians a price because of this bill to remove the freight rate subsidy on flour. So the Russians said to these Canadian millers "Tough cookie, we are going somewhere else since you cannot give us a price. You cannot tell us what the freight rate is going to be other than it will be higher, and since you want a higher price for your flour we are going somewhere else".
The same thing is going to happen with rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal. Our traditional customer, Japan, bought four shiploads from France last month because the Government of Canada sat. The Minister of Transport and the railroad want to do something to the statutory grain rates. What have they done to protect these traditional markets, Mr. Speaker? Not only have they done nothing to protect them but they are making efforts to endanger those markets further.
When the four western premiers met in Medicine Hat yesterday they called the decision of the cabinet on freight rates, on rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal, a doublecross. I say it is more than a doublecross, it is a betrayal. The Liberals in the last election, as well as after the election, promised that the anomalies in our freight rate structure would be removed. Yet exactly the opposite has happened, and it is happening again today. As if the United Grain Growers were not having enough trouble serving their own members and protecting them from the tender mercies of the international grain companies, the CPR and the Minister of Transport, we now have this sort of decision from the government which is going to make their difficulties even worse.
All members of the House support this bill and will see it through parliament quickly. But I remind the House that some of the motherhood remarks that came from the other side are more like crocodile tears. All of the other moves the government is making are going to do nothing but harm the western grain producers and co-operatives. The United Grain Growers and the other grain co-operatives are trying to raise capital to modernize and enlarge their country elevator system and their capacity to move our grain quickly, thus serving their members even better. Yet they have been continually kicked in the face.
Who was it, Mr. Speaker, who raised the subject of the Crowsnest rates? It was not the farmers, the wheat pools
April 29, 1976

or the United Grain Growers. Certainly the CPR has been complaining about them since 1899, but aside from that, who was it who raised the matter in recent years? It was the present Minister of Transport, the farmers' friend. He raised the subject two or three years ago in a speech in Winnipeg when he said possibly it was time to review the Crowsnest rates. There is only one way they can be reviewed, Mr. Speaker, and that is upwards. Certainly I cannot fathom the farmers asking that they be reviewed downwards.
Who was it, Mr. Speaker, who took feed grains out of the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board? We all know these fellows who say that the Canadian Wheat Board is the greatest thing since sliced bread, and they tell us how they support orderly marketing under the Canadian Wheat Board. But who was it who removed feed grains from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board? And, by the way, they were supported by the Tories. It was the Minister of Transport again, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. All of these actions have handicapped the United Grain Growers as well as the wheat pools of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Alberta, for decades.
I remind the shareholders and members of United Grain Growers that battles won do not necessarily stay won. So long as there are those who propose an antiquated, so-called free enterprise and open market system for grain, the gains and battles won by United Grain Growers, Sask Wheat Pool and the Farmers' Union to get orderly marketing, to build their own co-operatives and to market their own grain, will always remain in jeopardy. They will always have to be on their guard, fighting the same old enemies. Many of those same old enemies are still in the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker. We had a good example of this today when we found out what the cabinet has done about freight rates for rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal.
Historically we are not supposed to be able, according to successive Liberal and Tory governments, to manufacture and process our own production in western Canada. We are supposed to grow the raw product and send it to eastern Canada or the Pacific coast for manufacturing and processing. Then we buy it back, and it is very expensive. We are not going to stand for that in the prairie provinces, and the four western premiers made that very plain yesterday when they called this a doublecross. I am sure they did not use those words idly. The Premier of Alberta, speaking on behalf of the four premiers, last night made it very plain how western Canada feels about this kind of treatment.
What good are massive expenditures by the United Grain Growers or other wheat pools to improve even more their capacity to handle grain and process our agricultural products when we continue to get treatment in respect of transportation and orderly marketing such as we have been getting from this and previous governments? I hope this legislation not only passes but that the members and shareholders of the United Grain Growers repeat again the message they have been trying to get through to successive national governments regarding freight rates and orderly marketing. The overwhelming majority of grain producers in western Canada are unanimous about these issues. This is the message we have to get through to this government, and as long as we continue to have a so-called free enter-
United. Grain Growers
prise government of either of the old line parties the grain producers will have to continue to fight.
I commend this legislation to the House. I support it, my party supports it, and we will continue to support the co-operative movement set up on behalf of grain producers in western Canada and the producers of other agricultural commodities who have continually been having a job done on them. This is discrimination that we are sick and tired of, and we want to assure this parliament and this government that they have not heard the last from us and many others about this kind of discrimination.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a very few words about Bill S-33, and I certainly do not intend to take as long as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) in pointing out a gloomy picture as he did. I should like to talk for a few minutes about the company we are dealing with, namely, the United Grain Growers. I can probably say without too much fanfare, if you like, that I am probably the only person to speak during this debate who is actually a permit holder and has actually delivered grain to this particular elevator company.
It goes without saying, certainly on the part of most people in western Canada, especially farmers, that this company is viewed as one of the most progressive elevator companies and one of the most progressive farm companies in western Canada, and perhaps even in Canada itself. Certainly one of the good things about the United Grain Growers, which has been mentioned earlier, is the structure of that organization. It operates in some respects like a pool and in other respects like a private company. Because of this UGG has been able to get top-notch people into the top echelon of the company, bringing them up through the ranks to operate the day to day workings of the company.
This top echelon has a great deal of influence not only within the elevator system in which they operate but also in respect of farm policy which affects the farmers and, I suppose, ultimately all Canadians. The company has been instrumental in almost every progressive organization in western Canada in that its members of the board of directors hold prominent positions outside that board. I say this just to illustrate the influence that this particular elevator company has in western Canada.
Bill S-33 will be of great benefit and is certainly supported by the majority of members in the House. The increase in the capital is one of the major aspects of this piece of legislation. That additional capital will be required in the future because, whether we like it or not, there is going to be a drastic revision or change in elevator policy in coming years. There will be fewer elevators and they will be in all likelihood further apart. When the Hall Commission recommendations are implemented in western Canada there will be a tremendous change in our elevator or grain collecting system. The extra capital will definitely be needed, and I certainly recommend the passage of this bill to hon. members.
Let me take this opportunity to congratulate the United Grain Growers for the work it has done in western Canada and for being partly responsible for introducing competition to our grain handling system.

In spite of not coming from western Canada I am aware of the background of the United Grain Growers and the fact that it was started by a number of farmers co-operating among themselves many years ago. They developed this company long before there was an act in respect of co-operatives. If that were not so this measure might be dealt with in a different manner.

I am interested in a couple of sentences that I wonder whether western farmers understand, and I raise this matter because this is common to our legislative measures. These sentences are confusing. In the explanation to Clause 1 it is stated:
Notwithstanding subsection (2), the directors of the Company may, for any fiscal year, declare an additional dividend of one-half of one per centum, or any multiple thereof to a maximum of one and one-half per centum, of the par value of the Class "A" shares-
What is "per centum"? For many years in this country, since we stopped the compulsory study of Latin, we have dropped most of the Latin terms. I am sure there are some people who understand what that means, but I wonder how many-

motion No. 1:
That Bill C-68, An Act to amend the Medical Care Act, be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 1 to 16 at page 2.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we have spent quite some time on this bill which originally was debated last fall, if I recall correctly. I spent a good deal of time last summer getting ready for it because we thought it would be one of the first items of business, but here we are at the end of April and the bill is still before the House.
The reason for taking such a long time on this bill is that it has been subject to a substantial amount of controversy. We on this side of the House felt that it was a rather strange way of conducting federal-provincial relations in this country. At the time that the bill was first brought in last June during the budget debate, federal-provincial negotiations were in progress which were intended in some way to rearrange the cost sharing programs between the federal and provincial governments in so far as health care is concerned. Strangely enough, at that time it appeared that the provinces were satisfied that negotiations were being carried on in a satisfactory way.
A working committee was established to study the problem and bring in a report. While this committee had almost completed its work and was going to meet some time last September, the former minister of finance announced that the federal government had decided to take this unilateral and arbitrary action without further consultations with the provinces. It struck us as being a rather arrogant way, to say the least, of dealing with the provinces since, as I said, negotiations were being carried on at that time.
The minister has since made it quite clear in committee on many occasions that in his view the presentation and passage of this bill do not in any way interfere with the
Medical Care Act
conduct of negotiations which are still continuing. The minister assured us in committee that he feels that satisfactory progress is being made in terms of renegotiating the cost sharing agreements between the federal government and the provinces, and this led me to believe that this bill was a little premature and perhaps completely unnecessary.
However, evidence which was presented by the minister to the committee suggested that the provinces are not necessarily unhappy about the first two years. We also received evidence from the Medical Association of Canada suggesting that it is not all that unhappy about the first two years of the bill since it calls for increases of some 13 per cent in the first year following its passage, and 10.5 per cent in the following year.
In both cases those figures are perhaps sufficiently high that at least the medical association is not very concerned about it, although I think the provinces are concerned. They did not like the bill in the form in which it was passed at second reading. However, in view of the fact that the minister claims that this bill will not interfere with continuing ongoing talks with regard to readjusting the cost sharing agreements, we on this side of the House felt that if that is the case, then the bill is really unnecessary beyond a certain period of time. Given the fact that there is a real desire on the part of the provinces to conclude these talks and negotiations in a fairly reasonable time, and given the minister's stated desire to do the same, we felt that there was no need for this kind of legislation lasting beyond a period of two years. For that reason the amendment which I am now proposing calls for the termination of this legislation following that two year period.
In committee the minister expressed some reservations about the amendment, on the one hand stating that negotiations were moving along fairly well, but on the other hand suggesting that he did not think any significant progress would be made by the time two years went by. That led one to be somewhat suspicious with regard to the seriousness with which he is conducting these negotiations. That took me right back to the beginning of our attack on the federal government for putting forward such legislation in the first place, which takes the approach that the provinces are not very important in so far as their opinions are concerned, that the federal government will play God, set the rules unilaterally and impose them on the provinces whether the provinces like them or not, and impose them on the people providing medical care whether they like it or not.
I think this method of approaching unity and federal-provincial relations is contrary to the spirit upon which this country was built. It seems to me that in a country such as ours consisting of a number of provinces and territories with their own governments, each with its own areas of responsibility, and a central government which also has its area of responsibility, where there is a situation involving cross-jurisdiction in certain areas, in order for Confederation to work adequately and in order for unity to be strong between the provinces or between the various regions of the country, there has to exist a feeling of mutual trust between the federal government and the provinces. In saying this we have to keep in mind the fact

Virtually all of the provinces, except for one, I think, objected to it when it was first introduced. They did not want it. They felt that they were already providing adequate medical insurance and that the introduction of the medicare act at that time was interfering with their own priorities. The provinces were forced to readjust their priorities quite drastically, and at that time they foresaw what was going to happen. They wondered how they could be sure that the federal government, once it imposed this program, realized the cost of it and realized the difficulty in controlling the cost, would not try to back out and leave them saddled with the burden of the whole cost. Indeed this is what appears to be happening. The feeling of trust, which I think once existed, has been severely damaged, and I am concerned about that because I do not want to see any more strain on Confederation than is absolutely necessary.
However, unfortunately we have a government before us, temporarily occupying the other side of the House, which has always taken this kind of approach to federal-provincial relations, the approach where consultation usually means making a unilateral decision and telling the provinces about it later. Sometimes it does not even do that; sometimes it makes a unilateral decision and issues a press release about it, and the provinces find out, by watching the 11 o'clock news or perhaps reading the local newspapers, what are the plans of the federal government.
I want to place this serious concern I have before the House and before the people of the country. If unity is to be maintained we must accept the fact that the feeling of trust which must exist between the various governments is something which should be protected. I am afraid the action the minister took in this regard did anything but protect that feeling of trust. Indeed I think that feeling was damaged quite substantially.
The minister still has an opportunity to recoup lost graces, if he wants to be graceful. He has an opportunity to tell the provinces that he has confidence in his own ability to negotiate with them and confidence in their desire to try to reach agreement with him through negotiation and consultation, and if he has that kind of confidence I am sure he will accept this motion which would have the effect of terminating the bill after a two year period.
I think I will just leave it at that. I have clearly outlined the reason for this motion. We debated this bill for a long time at second reading, and there was a reason for that. We have found, through long and difficult experience, that regardless of how good a point we want to make or how right we may be, generally speaking nobody on the government side listens to what we say. Either they do not listen or perhaps their skulls are rather thick. I am not sure which it is. In any case, we find that by repeating something over and over again ad infinitum, sometimes it eventually sinks in. So here we are once again repeating things which have already been said. I know the minister sometimes listens while he is doing other things. He assured me at one time that he can talk to two or three people and listen to a speech at the same time.

We get the impression that this particular government always takes the position that it alone represents the views of the people, that it alone can come up with ideas beneficial to Canada. For some reason it takes the position that parties on this side of the House have never come up with a good idea. I take objection to that position of course. Every member on this side of the House has fought an election, as have members on the other side. Every member on this side of the House represents the views of a certain segment of the Canadian people; every member does his job by presenting the views of the people who elected him to this House.
I can never comprehend why we have so much difficulty making the government understand that improvements to legislation are always possible. We know it is easy to criticize and we know too that in our parliamentary system, where the adversary system is in effect, that we have a duty to criticize legislation put forward by the government and to point out any pitfalls that might exist. We know, of course, that members of the government would never do that. We know from experience that they stand up and repeat the same old drivel about how great they are, what good ideas they have, and what their legislation will do for the country. In the face of that we have an obligation to point out the truth and to offer suggestions on how legislation can be improved.
I think we have fulfilled that task over and over again in regard to this bill. We have offered many suggestions to make it more palatable to the people who would be affected by it. We have offered suggestions which would lead to a greater feeling of unity in the country, a feeling that the federal government is truly interested in co-operating with the provinces and, through the democratic process, reaching a solution acceptable to the largest number of Canadians.
I will conclude by saying again that if the minister is sincere in his desire to consult meaningfully with the provinces, this bill will be totally unnecessary by the time two years have expired. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) pointed out that this debate has been going on for a long time. It really started last June when the then minister of finance, Mr. Turner, gave notice of the government's intention to impose ceilings on the amount that the federal government would pay to the provinces in respect of medical care. The bill itself, of course, came in later.
There was a long debate at second reading which was brought to an end by the imposition of closure. We have since debated the bill in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. In that committee certain amendments were made, and I notice that in addition to the report stage amendments proposed from this side of the House there is now a further amendment by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) also being proposed at report stage.
I have to say, sir, that even with the amendments that the government made in the standing committee and with the amendment that the minister would make at this stage, Bill C-68 is still totally unacceptable to us. In our view one of the important advances that was made in Canada-and it took an awfully long time for that advance to be made- was when we established the principle of medical care for all our people, and when we made it a Canadian plan in the sense that the federal government would share the costs of medical care faced by the provinces in such a way as to provide equality of treatment and relative equality to the provinces right across Canada.
Now the government has come along and given notice that it is backing away from principles in this area and related areas which were forward steps. It is not only backing away from the formula for the financing of medical care which is represented in the bill now before us, it has also given notice to the provinces that at the end of this decade it will seek to renegotiate agreements regarding hospitalization. It is also in the process of cutting back on the funding of scientific research generally and medical research in particular.
No matter how much the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) might preach the need for restraint, no matter what problems we face in this country, we do not accept the idea of taking backward steps with respect to the provision of medical care for the people of Canada.
The bill that is now before us, as amended on the motion of the government in the standing committee, provides that in the first two years covered by the bill there are fixed limits as to the amount of increase that the provinces can expect from the government with respect to medical care.
Spokesmen on the government side like to make the point that these very increases indicate that the government is not paying out fewer dollars for medical care but
Medical Care Act
is, rather, prepared to pay out more dollars and that therefore those of us who cry havoc about this bill and try to contend that it involves a cutback are not "telling it as it
is".
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that one has to compare what will happen under this bill with what would happen if it were not enacted at all. If this bill were not enacted the federal government, under the Medical Care Act, would be required to pay the provinces roughly 50 per cent of their medical costs. Under this bill, with costs going up, the government will pay the lesser of two amounts, either 50 per cent of what it costs the provinces, or the number of dollars that were paid to them last year, plus a certain additional amount.
Since medicare started the provinces have been able to count on 50 per cent of those costs being paid by the federal government. I say 50 per cent, although I recognize that there is a formula that results in some provinces getting a little more, and some a little less; but the average is 50 per cent. The provinces that have been able to count on that will in future, if this bill is passed, not be able to count on getting 50 per cent of the costs of medical care. This bill fixes a precise limit in the first two years of the operation of this law. After that it is left to the government to decide by order in council.
The original bill brought before the House had precise figures in it for the next three years as well. The minister contended that he was doing something generous by taking out those figures and putting in the provision for the decision to be made by order in council. It means, if this bill goes through, that we have no way of knowing, and the provinces will have no way of knowing, what limits the government will impose after the first two years have gone
by-
It is well established, both in the language of the bill and in the minister's statements made in this House and in committee that, although there will be consultations with the provinces-and consultation is defined one way in the dictionary and in quite another way by this government- the provinces will have no real say. In the end the federal minister will make the decision and put it into effect by order in council.
So we have this picture: for two years the provinces will know the limits; they will also know that they will get less than the 50 per cent they have been getting. The provinces know that after that they will be completely at the mercy of the federal minister, who will be free to act by order in council.
The hon. member for Athabasca did well tonight, as he did on second reading, in pointing out that this is hardly the way to carry on federal-provincial relations. It is hardly the thing to do to get the provinces to come into a plan like this, get their system built up as it were, and then undercut them by making changes in the formula of the kind being proposed. We think it is wrong and unfair to the people of Canada who deserve the benefits of health care; we think it is wrong to treat the provinces this way. I suspect the minister knows better than we do, because he was at the conference, of the unhappiness of provincial

ministers of health because of the way the government has treated the provinces in the last number of years.
We do not like Bill C-68. We are against it, lock, stock, and barrel-all the way. Even so we are going to vote for the motion just proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca. It is a compromise. We would rather not have the bill at all, with its limitations; but if the motion proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca were to pass, and I hope it will, there would be the ceilings the provinces already know about for the first two years, but after that this limiting bill would have no further effect. After that we would return to the provisions of the original Medical Care Act.
As I say, Sir, we would much rather not see the limitations imposed by the government in those first two years; alternatively, it certainly would be better if the legislation could go only that far, if there could be limitations for only two years after which we could return to the principles laid down in the Medical Care Act itself. In other words, if the motion proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca is accepted by the House we would know what would happen for two years, after which we should be governed again by the principles of the original legislation. For this reason we welcome the proposal made by the hon. member for Athabasca. In this he would probably agree with me; I expect he would rather not have limitations in those two years; he would rather see the whole bill treated as I have suggested, made into a bill which would self-destruct, so to speak, and put into the minister's hands for that process. I hope that the minister and the House might consider that as a compromise.
If we cannot persuade the government to drop the idea altogether, that is, of walking away for the 50 per cent provision in the Medical Care Act, the compromise at least would impose those limitations only for the first two years. For this reason I shall be glad to see lines 1 to 16 on page 2 of the bill deleted. The proposal moved by the hon. member for Athabasca calls for just that.
Sir, I have already referred to the important milestone which was reached when medical care on a national basis was established in this country. I must be careful not to make a speech I have made many times in this House, about the great Liberal party of 1919 and the great things to which it committed itself, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and health insurance. One could find that speech of mine in a great many volumes of Hansard. It tells the story of the years it took to achieve these things to which the Liberals committed themselves in 1919. And if I condemned them for taking so long, I gave them credit for moving in the right direction.
I cannot for the life of me understand why the Liberals, who were finally dragged into doing those progressive things for the people of Canada, now want to water them down. Health care for the people of Canada on a free, universal basis is a good idea. It is one of the best things that marks life in this country. To jeopardize it in this way is to betray the people of Canada. Certainly it is a betrayal of those Liberals of bygone decades who dreamed of achieving this sort of thing.
We again appeal to the government to scrap this bill completely. If it is not prepared to do that, I plead with the minister to accept motion No. 1 proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca, and call a halt to imposing ceilings

after the first two years. Mr. Speaker, we shall support the motion proposed by the hon. member for Athabasca.

My colleague from Winnipeg North says they have been trying to forget them every since.
That was a great convention. It was the convention at which Mr. Mackenzie King was elected leader of the party. In the main speech he made at that convention, not a speech in the leadership contest itself, but in terms of dealing with policy matters, he dealt with the resolution that had been brought in calling for the three things I mentioned a while ago; old age pensions, unemployment insurance and health insurance. Mr. King called on the Liberal party of that day to commit itself to these things and to set out to make the Canada of the post-war world- that was after World War I-the better place it could be if we had old age pensions, unemployment insurance, and health insurance. It took a long while to get them.
It was not until 1926 that the old age pension law got on to the statute books so that it could come into effect in 1927. I was not until 1940 that unemployment insurance was passed. It looked for a time as though the third of those three things was going to be forgotten altogether. However, every once in a while we would remind Mr. King of the speech he made in 1919. He always came back and said he was going to see it implemented all the way, but things could not be done overnight.
It was not long before he quit being Prime Minister-I think it was about 1947 or 1948-that this place was a-buzz one day because an announcement on health was coming from the Prime Minister, one of those statements on motions. We even dared to believe that it was the beginning of health insurance. It turned out not to be that. However, it did turn out to be a program of hospital grants which he said would lay the foundation of health insurance later on. Well, that later on still had some years to come.
It was not until just before the Liberals went out of office in 1957 that they got hospitalization on to the statute books. Even so they had a provision or rider that prevented it from coming into effect. Of all things, it took the Progressive Conservatives to amend that bill so that hospitalization could come into effect. A few years later the Liberals came back and, in the days of Mr. Pearson as Prime Minister, we finally got health insurance, the Medical Care Act, on to the statute books.
That is a long story. I think I can be given credit for telling it in such a few minutes. I was telling the story of the period from 1919 to the middle sixties. That is the time it took to get this legislation on to the books. I was critical through the years I was here about how slow the process was, and how inadequate some of the provisions were that got enacted. However, these were all moves in the right direction of a better Canada for those who count, namely, the people of this country.
One of the hallmarks of that legislation is the provision for medical care. As I have already said, not only is it medical care that has been provided, but it has been provided on a basis that fits the Canadian scene in that the federal government pays half the cost and the provinces do the administering.

We now have before us legislation stipulating that despite the provisions of the Medical Care Act there will be this limitation that provinces will get 50 per cent, though not if their costs go up to the point where they exceed so many dollars more than they got the previous year. We think that this is an unfair way to treat the provinces. It is not the way to bring about co-operation. We also think that if it is done in this way some of the poorer provinces will be faced with special problems and will either have to cut back on the amount of medical care they can provide, or institute deterrent fees, extra taxes, or one thing or another, and then we will soon have the situation where the provision of health care is unequal across Canada, being better in some parts than in others.
We think the whole concept of a limitation as contained in this bill is wrong and ought to be stopped in its tracks. We said that right away last June when Mr. Turner brought in his budget. I can tell the House, if one is permitted in this place to refer to political conventions, that at the national convention of the New Democratic Party held in Winnipeg last July one of the things that concerned our delegates most was the Turner threat to cut back on hospital and medical care. Certainly I speak for my colleagues in our party when I say we do not want this to happen.
Having admitted that the Liberals have brought us to a certain point which was worth while, I simply cannot understand why they now want to reverse the situation. One of the arguments that is used is that if it is an open-ended situation, as it is now, then the provinces will spend money hog wild on medical care. But they have to pay the other 50 per cent. I point out that they are as concerned about achieving economy as is the federal government, and they have made the point to the minister that there are better ways than this.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, we think the whole idea of imposing limits that result in the provinces getting less money than they would get under the Medical Care Act is wrong. My hope is that the House will accept this motion of mine which in effect wipes out the whole idea contained in Bill C-68. If we cannot do that, I hope we will at least accept the proposal that is made in the previous motion No. 1 and stop this process of cutting off funds for medical care after two years have gone by.
I have already said, and perhaps my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), may develop this a little more, that this, to us, is frightening when there is associated with it cutbacks in funding for scientific and medical research. To us, Mr. Speaker, the government seems to be moving in so many directions to make life harder for people. Using the excuse of restraint not to increase family allowances is part of the picture. Cutbacks in social services that are being made in the provinces because of the government's attitude toward federal and provincial fiscal arrangements are wrong. Therefore all down the line we are opposed to Bill C-68. My motion No. 3, which we are now discussing, if it passes would take out of the bill the whole of that part of the bill that imposes limits on what the federal government can pay to the provinces. Therefore I hope the House will vote in favour of this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I have no intention of repeating at length the arguments that I put forward at earlier stages of this bill. I rise mainly because, despite all of the protestations of the minister, the facts are exactly as they were when the bill was discussed months ago.
The provinces, which will be so adversely affected by the unilateral decision of the government as outlined in the bill and by other proposals that the government is going to make, are still adamantly and unanimously opposed to the basic principle contained in this bill. Indeed on Tuesday and Wednesday of this week the provincial ministers of health were in Ottawa meeting with their federal colleague and I know-and I am sure the minister will not challenge my statement-that they are still unanimously opposed to this bill.
If one looks at this bill and at the other proposals that the government has announced it will implement in the very near future having to do with estimates in various fields, it is not surprising that the Conservative provincial governments of Newfoundland, Ontario and Alberta, the Liberal governments of Prince Edward Island and Quebec, the NDP governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and the Social Credit government of British Columbia all oppose the principle of this particular bill as well as the other proposals to which I have referred. They do so because what they see is a pattern that has ominous implications for the provinces. After all, Mr. Speaker, with respect to virtually all of the social legislation we have and virtually all the other legislation in the field of health and welfare-I would use the term "blackmail" except it may be unparliamentary-the pressure for implementation mostly came from the federal government.
What do we see now, Mr. Speaker? In this bill the federal government is proposing to place limits on specific increases for the next two years which it will pay under the 50-50 sharing arrangement of health care costs. The federal government has given notice that it will opt out of the 50-50 cost sharing of hospital insurance in 1980, which is the first time it can get out of the present agreement.
The federal government is proposing a social services act which will wipe out the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan, and although the provinces do not yet know all the details this will mean that the provinces will be saddled with a substantially larger part of the costs. I see the minister shaking his head. It is easy for him to shake his head in this House when he has a big majority behind him, but I know that he has not convinced his provincial counterparts that this will not be the effect of the social services act. The minister can shrug his shoulders and wave his hand at me, but I have talked to some of his provincial counterparts and they all tell me the same thing.

speechtext:
Someone says "Give them the bucks, that is all they want". Of course that is all they want, because the bucks come from the same source-the pockets of the Canadian people.
Whether we are dealing with federal, provincial or municipal financing, the question is: which level of gov-
April 29, 1976

ernment has the constitutional and practical authority and ability to raise taxes in the most equitable way? Any member of parliament with any common sense, and I exempt the member who interjected a few moments ago as he has demonstrated he has very little common sense, and any member who can look at problems objectively will admit that the level of government least able to meet its expenses is the municipal level.
The next level of government least able to meet its expenses in any field is the provincial level, whether it be the have-not provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia or Quebec, or the have provinces such as Ontario or British Columbia. If the hon. member does not believe me he ought to listen to what the Liberal premier of Nova Scotia has been saying about costs and the impossible task of the people of Nova Scotia in paying their extremely high electric power costs because of the high price of oil. If the hon. member does not believe me then let him wait to see what happens to the Liberal party at the next provincial or federal election.
The government which is most able to find money for necessary programs is the federal government because of its ability to tax those who have the money, yet it is the federal government that is getting out of these cost-sharing programs as fast as it can. I could go on talking about how the federal government is cutting back on services which it has provided over the years to the native people who move off reserves. There is no member here who can deny that. The federal government is doing everything possible to get out of its constitutional and moral obligation to provide health and welfare services to our native people.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests I might say a few words about the record of this federal government in the field of medical research. This is obviously an important aspect in the total cost of medical care. If our medical researchers can make a breakthrough in respect of one of the major illnesses that strike so many Canadian people, be it cancer, a stroke, or any one of the many, this would mean a very sharp reduction in the cost of health care.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is putting a freeze on the very small amount of money the federal government provides for medical research. This is not the time to put the entire case on the record, but what is it that our medical researchers are asking? Are they talking in terms of billions of dollars, hundreds of millions of dollars, or even tens of millions of dollars? Our medical researchers are talking about the tremendous amount of $4.5 million. But the Minister of National Health and Welfare has the gall and the audacity to tell our medical researchers that the Canadian people cannot afford that kind of money.
Let us look at some of the things we have been able to afford. We might consider the $2 billion we have spent on Mirabel, and we might consider the $1,275 million the Canadian people will have spent on the Olympics before we are finished. We might also consider the tremendous increase in the number of civil servants who are at the top level of our bureaucratic system receiving from $30,000 to
Medical Care Act
$65,000 a year. This number has almost tripled in a half a dozen years. The minister and his colleagues have been able to find the money for these things, but not for medical research.
We have the spectacle of the federal government saying to the provinces that it simply cannot afford to continue the 50-50 sharing of health care costs. Indeed the federal government is making an effort to get out of the 50-50 sharing of hospital insurance costs as soon as it can, in spite of the fact it has been obvious for many years that in the field of hospital insurance Ottawa has been more than willing to pay 50 per cent of the most expensive kind of hospital care, and that is for the active care hospitals. The federal government has not been willing until now to pay any share of the cost of health care in nursing homes, convalescent homes, and other similar types of institutions. As a result the provinces have carried that cost alone. This is the least costly form of medical care. The federal government has been willing to pay for the more expensive care.
I am sure there is not a member of parliament who has not come in contact with individuals who are occupying active or acute hospital beds when they really do not need to remain under active treatment. They could very well be at home, in a nursing or convalescent home, but very often the city in which they live does not have that kind of facility. In any event, that kind of care is not covered by insurance.
It would be much less expensive for taxpayers as a whole to provide for that alternative type medical care. This is not the case now because under the present schemes the individual or his family must pay the entire cost of that type of care. I am sure there is not one member of parliament who has not known of a constituent who has said at some time that he or his mother, or his father, or his cousin, or his aunt, should not be occupying an active bed in hospital. They will tell you that the alternative service is not available or, that if it is available they persuade the doctor to let patient stay in the hospital because the individual or the family would have to pay for that alternative service. The federal government has not had the will or the flexibility to co-operate with the provinces in meeting the alternative.
I have said in earlier speeches, and I repeat again, that the provinces are even more concerned about spiralling costs of health and hospital care services than the federal government because they do not have the ability to meet the increased costs like the federal government has in Ottawa. The provinces are not undertaking expensive luxury programs that the federal government has undertaken, some of which I have referred to already.
The provincial authorities know what it means to go to their citizens when costs of medical care increase by more than 13 per cent, which is what will be permitted under the provisions of this bill. All of these provincial levels of government are trying very seriously to find ways to slow down the growth if not the actual expenditures, and they ought to have the co-operation of the federal government in this regard. Experts in this field working for the federal government should sit down with provincial authorities to work out ways of cutting down on expenses.
