If there are some governments which have been slow in beginning to look at ways of reducing increasing costs, surely the minister's department should have been willing and able to provide those recalcitrant provinces with the expertise to find ways. We have seen none of this co-operation from the federal government. What we have seen is simply a unilateral decision on the part of Ottawa to cut its share of increasing health care costs.
The allowed increases are to be 13 per cent in the coming year and 10 per cent the year after that. Following that, what the minister proposes is that the increase in succeeding years will be left to the tender mercies of the federal government. In light of the experiences the provinces have had with the federal government it is not surprising that, to say the least, they have been loathe to leave this decision to its tender mercies. As I have indicated, they have unanimously rejected the federal government's proposal. They have called on the minister to stand his bill over and wait until the next couple of months when the provincial ministers concerned meet with their federal counterparts in order to work out a program that is mutually agreeable to all the provinces and the federal government, whereby co-operatively the increases which have taken place can be moderated.
It is because I believe the arguments put forward by the provinces are justified that I, and other members of the NDP, have opposed this bill from the day it was suddenly announced. It was announced unilaterally and without any consultation. Indeed it was announced really in violation of the spirit of the discussions which had taken place between the minister and his provincial counterparts just a few months before the infamous budget of June, 1975.
All the discussions which have taken place since last June between the minister and his provincial counterparts, and all the discussions which have taken place here have demonstrated to me that the provinces were right, and that the provinces have been much more aware and concerned about the needs of the people who are citizens not only of the provinces in which they reside but also of Canada. Because I am convinced the provinces have been right and the federal government has been wrong I intend to vote for this motion. If the motion should be defeated, as I suppose it will, I propose to oppose the passage of Bill C-68, as I have from the beginning, in the belief that eventually even this government will realize its mistake.
I wish to conclude by saying that in the spare time I have had I have been re-reading some Canadian history. It seems obvious to me that when the history of this era comes to be written, historians in assessing the Canadian governments which have been in office since 1940 will find that this Liberal government led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been the most reactionary, conservative government we have had in the last 50 years.

Having spoken earlier in the debate on Bill C-68 I have said many of the things I might have said

at this time. However, there are one or two things I have previously indicated to the minister during the committee hearings which I think he has thoroughly overlooked. In a sense I think he is defrauding the people of Canada by not looking at some of the serious aspects of payment for medical care.
We have heard quite a bit tonight about the history of health care in Canada, both from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and more recently the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I am sure both members have much to be proud of in a sense at this stage in history, but I say that history will tell an entirely different story in 50 or 100 years when we have the virtual collapse or decay of our society because of the way in which we are spoiling people by not giving them an opportunity to exercise responsibility and self-reliance.
I wish to refer to the action of the government over the years in which this legislation has been in effect. As I mentioned previously, it was introduced by the Liberal government of five or six years ago contrary to the wishes of some of the provinces. Certainly from the viewpoint of the province of Ontario it represented an insidious tax which would have taken a lot of money from the province if it did not agree to go along with the scheme. Now, having been taken in with respect to this medical care bill, the province finds itself in the position of being forced to pay more because the federal contribution is to be drastically cut in the future. This appears to be a unilateral action on the part of the government which I believe is uncalled for. As the previous speakers have said, there is not one province at this time which is in agreement with this. It seems too bad that this is being forced on them once again.
What I wish to speak about mainly has to do with what I believe is one of the principal deficiencies in the thinking and the philosophy of the minister in respect of the provision of health care in Canada. It is obvious that he is attempting to save costs, particularly for the federal treasury. I do not fault the minister for that. However, we should look at the four criteria set down by the government. The first is universality. The second is comprehensiveness. The third is portability, and the fourth is public control of costs.
I submit that the government has omitted one very important aspect of control. I refer to patient control. Having been a practising physician for a number of years it is obvious now to me, having worked under medical care for years, that the best control of cost in respect of health care is not the computer in the local insurance office in the provincial capital but rather the patient himself or herself. It is the patient who is the best monitor of the cost of health care services. If we recognize that, not only will we keep down the cost but we will also provide a social favour to the people of this country which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in my view, fails to recognize in his deep concern for humanity.
I suggest there is no reason why the government could not institute another criterion in the provision of medical care services which would include the involvement of the patient in his own health care, in a way in which this is not provided for at the present time. One simple way to provide this kind of involvement is for the physician to bill
April 29, 1976

the patient directly and have the patient pay the physician. That happens to be the official policy of the Ontario Medical Association, the largest association of its kind in this country. It is a very wise policy. Unfortunately for various reasons very few physicians across the country like to adhere to that policy, sometimes for selfish reasons. The same is true sometimes in respect of the patient, the consumer.
It has been my experience and my confirmed belief that if we could somehow involve the patients in their own health care, they would appreciate the cost of these services. As it is now the patient seldom realizes the bill that is being incurred on his or her behalf when patients visit their physician. This is certainly unfortunate and does not lead to any kind of control.
I am concerned about the way society in Canada is going. One can see a gradual decay, an internal rot setting in which I think stems from a number of factors, but one of the principal factors is that we do not encourage our people to provide for themselves. We tend to think that a big government can do things better than individuals can. I would be the first to agree that there is a small number of people in our society who are unable to provide for themselves, and of course we need to have appropriate health care and medical plans which will give those people the kind of services they need. By the same token, with the rising cost of health care and the increasing availability of more esoteric types of medical services, and the fact that we all feel we are entitled to them, there is no doubt health care costs are rising.
When one is sick it is difficult to meet bills, and I would be the first to agree that we must have some type of insurance scheme available. If it is provided by the state I see nothing wrong with that, although there have been many private plans that have been equally good and perhaps better, and run at much less cost to the consumer. So I feel that if we are going to do any kind of favour for the people of Canada as they progress into future generations, we must do something to provide an independence for people and to teach them how to look after themselves.
For some reason there is a notion around the country, which I think has been propagated mainly by politicians because they find they can get votes by advocating comprehensive, universal types of plans, that health care is some God-given right that everybody has, as if the individual had no responsibility to provide it for himself. There are many other essential services that all of us need and which we are continually using, as essential as health care, and yet few of us think they should be supplied in total by the state. Who would ever think that we should all have housing provided at no cost to ourselves except through a small premium or taxation?

I think I have to take a moment to summarize the whole position which is before the House tonight, as I see it. We have a bill which provides for the limiting of the contributions of the federal government to the provinces in respect of medicare, commencing now. The bill, as we now have it, provides for precise limits for two years, and then for limits to be determined by order in council unilaterally by the government after those first two years. I have already said that in my view the whole bill should be ditched. I think that these limits should not apply even in the first two years. That is the first position, and I have taken it by putting down my motion, notion No. 3.

The second course is that contained in motion No. 1 in the name of the hon. member for Athabasca which accepts the cuts for the first two years and then wants no more cuts in succeeding years. That is not as good as my motion, but it is the next best position.
However, then we have two other propositions: the one which is before us now in motion No. 2, and the one which will be before us later in motion No. 4. The proposal in motion No. 2, which is now before us, is that if the government by order in council sets any limits after the first two years, year by year that order in council cannot come into effect until the House of Commons has had a chance to vote on it. Motion No. 2 asks for an affirmative vote before that action takes place. That has some meaning, although not a great deal when there is a government with the majority this government has, and with the characteristics this government has, because it would simply mean a debate, and then the motion would carry. However, at least parliament would have a chance to decide on those limitations before they come into effect.
In a few minutes the minister will try to propose an alternative, namely, that if the government brings in an order in council setting limits, it should come into effect right away, but if 50 members sign their names to a motion, the minister will let parliament afterward debate whether it should have come into effect, and only if a majority in parliament is against it can the order in council be declared to be without effect. I think the difference between the motion now before us and the motion which will come in the name of the minister is the difference between night and day. One would give parliament a chance to say something at a point where it might be effective. The other would give parliament a chance to try to lock the barn door after the horse has been stolen.
The hon. member for Athabasca and I have been seeing eye to eye and saying the same things all night. I plead with him to toughen up a bit and not accept motion No. 4 as a compromise for his motion No. 2. If we cannot have my proposal to kill the bill completely, or if we cannot have the proposal in motion No. 1 that the cut-offs die at the end of two years, then I think the next best thing we should have is what is set out in the motion now before us, namely, that if there is an order in council in years 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7 down the road, before such order in council can come into effect it has to be brought before parliament for a decision by this House of Commons.
Therefore I am in favour of and we shall vote for motion No. 2.

(2)	Where an order of the Governor in Council has been laid before the House of Commons pursuant to subsection (1), a notice of motion in the House of Commons signed by not less than fifty members thereof and made in accordance with the rules of that House within seven days of the day the order was laid before that House praying that the order be revoked shall be taken up and considered in that House at the first convenient opportunity within the four sitting days next after the day the motion in that House was made.
(3)	At fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on the second sitting day following the commencement of consideration of a motion of which notice was given under subsection (2), or at such earlier time as the House of Commons is ready for the question, the Speaker shall put the question forthwith without further debate.
(4)	If a motion considered by the House of Commons pursuant to this section is adopted by the House, with or without amendments, a message shall be sent to the Senate informing the Senate that the motion has been so adopted and requesting that the motion be concurred in by the Senate.
(5)	The Senate shall, within the first four days next after receipt by it of a request from the House of Commons pursuant to subsection (4) that the Senate is sitting, in accordance with the Rules of the Senate, take up and consider the motion adopted by the House of Commons that is the subject of the request and all questions in connection therewith shall be debated without interruption and decided not later than the end of the third sitting day next after the day the motion is first so taken up and considered.
(6)	If the Senate, pursuant to a request from the House of Commons, concurs in a motion adopted by the House as provided in this section, the order of the Governor in Council to which the motion relates is thereupon revoked effective from the day on which it was made.

He said: I thank hon. members for having agreed to consider these various motions tonight and for their contributions to the debate. I realize that various amendments have been brought forward to ensure that the points cov-

April 29, 1976
Medical Care Act
ered in committee will once again be discussed by the House at report stage. They represent the views of the opposition parties on this bill. Although I do not agree and the government does not agree with the amendments, I am convinced they are brought forward in a constructive way and with the best of intentions.
If I were to take the points that have been raised on this bill tonight, there are three or four that I should like to spend a couple of minutes on and then say a few words about motion No. 4.
There has been a complaint of unilateral action by the government in this case because the decision was brought in by a budget in June, 1975, by the former minister of finance. I have already covered some of that ground in committee, but I would remind hon. members again that after this particular announcement was made I had extensive consultation with the provinces and with the Canadian Medical Association. Following those consultations several amendments were made to the bill. As a matter of fact the bill before us is substantially different from the bill presented for first reading. Those changes were made following consultations and discussions with the provinces and the Canadian Medical Association. Obviously they do not meet all the points raised by the provinces and the CMA but they certainly go some way to meeting some of the concerns that have been expressed.
In addition, motion No. 4 is a change that the government is ready to support in order to take account of some of the views expressed by members of the opposition. As the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) said, motion No. 4 is substantially in the same spirit, as the motion brought forward by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco). In this particular instance, therefore, the government has shown a lot of consideration for the views expressed on this bill. Obviously we have not withdrawn the bill; we believe the bill is necessary and that it is appropriate in the circumstances.
The hon. member for Athabasca put forward a motion to the effect that we should have this bill only for the first two years, on the basis that the provinces and the Canadian Medical Association did not seem to object too much to that proposition. I will admit to the hon. member that possibly Bill C-68 might not be necessary after the first two years. Several eventualities might occur in the meantime which would render it unnecessary. As a matter of fact I would hope that the government would not have to use the provisions of the bill after the first two years. That is why, instead of putting in a specific maximum contribution by the federal government, we have brought forward an amendment which leaves it to be decided by order in council after consultation with the provinces.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that there is no requirement for the government to put such a limit on the increase of its contribution. It may very well be, therefore, that after consultation with the provinces we will find that their plans for the following year are reasonable in the circumstances and that there does not appear to be any need to provide for a specific ceiling on the rate of increase of the cost of medical care. If, together with the provinces, we can develop an adequate control on the rate of increase in costs, then recourse to order in council would not be necessary.

It may very well be that in the next two years we and the provinces will have arrived at a general financing formula which will replace both the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and the Medical Care Act.
For the past two days I have presided at a conference with my provincial colleagues. The feeling amongst the provincial ministers was that following the meeting of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with the premiers in June we should try to develop a new health financing formula to replace both existing pieces of legislation and bring in a new technique for cost sharing. If this were to be accomplished and there were early agreement between the federal government and the provinces, obviously Bill C-68 would disappear. Not only would it self-destruct to use the hon. member for Athabasca's expression, but the Medical Care Act would be replaced in such an eventuality.
I am not saying that after two years the federal government would necessarily adopt orders in council setting some ceilings on the rate of increase in cost of medicare; on the other hand, however, it would be inappropriate for the federal government not to provide for the possibility that such agreement on a new financing formula would not have taken place or the possibility that agreement would not be reached with the provinces on what should be an adequate rate of growth of the cost of medicare. If that were to be the case, we feel that there should be in the hands of the federal government some power, as is provided in the present act, to put a ceiling on the rate of increase of the federal contribution.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) felt that such a measure was extremely wrong and unfair to the provinces. I was rather surprised to hear him use such strong words, Mr. Speaker. In effect, since the inception of hospital insurance and medicare we have seen the provinces deciding on their own how much the federal government was going to pay without consultation with the federal government, and without the federal government having anything to say about how much the bill would be at the end of the year. We are committed to paying 50 per cent of whatever the provinces decide to spend, and at no time do we have an idea of how much we are going to be asked to contribute, until we have received the last bill from the provinces.
In effect we shall now know what kind of bill to expect from the provinces. We have never said it is wrong or unfair, or used the kinds of adjectives used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in describing this bill. This bill pays more respect to the role of respective governments than present legislation does, no matter whether we talk of hospital insurance or medical care. Indeed, it provides for the ceiling to be set after consultation with provinces.
The provinces will know ahead of time what they can expect as a maximum contribution from the federal government. They therefore will be able to plan the expenditures they will incur and the kind of settlements they can make with the medical profession, as well as arrangements they will need to make for meeting the total expense of medical care. They can plan all this well ahead of time, something which the federal government has not been able
April 29, 1976

to do in the past, as we were asked to pay the bill afterwards.
An hon. member called this bill a backward step. It is some "backward step". I calculated quickly how much more, not less, the federal government is expected to contribute next year to medical care alone under the present bill. This bill calls on the federal government to cost-share with the provinces next year the small additional sum of about $250 million for medicare alone. If that is a backward step, I do not know what the hon. member would call a forward step. We are not talking about cutting or reducing our contribution to medical care. We say that we shall have better control of the rate of growth, of the rate of escalation of our contributions to medical care. Therefore in that sense many of the statements made in committee and on second reading are exaggerated, especially when you consider the choices this bill provides.
Some hon. members talked of the opposition of the provinces to this bill. This was also raised in committee. Indeed it would be surprising if the provinces were to welcome this provision since it will do away with the blank cheque arrangement of the past. Now the provinces will know ahead of time how much they can draw from the federal government for medical care. I suppose if most of us could choose between having a blank cheque to draw any amount, and being told ahead of time how much we can draw, most of us would choose the blank cheque. The provinces are reacting just as individuals would react in those circumstances. That is the change we propose.
Some hon. members mention medical research, an area of concern to me and the government. I said previously that I am reviewing carefully the whole situation to see if we cannot find funds with which to alleviate the present difficulties of medical research. That, of course, is not the subject of this bill. I understand that the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs is to consider the estimates of my department soon. Witnesses on behalf of the medical research community will appear, and we shall have the opportunity to consider this issue at greater length.
Finally, let me say that the government is not backing away from cost-sharing. As I have already mentioned, this bill does not reduce the contribution of the federal government. Next year, for medicare alone, it will increase it by as much as $250 million for both levels of government. The social services bill will be proposed later this year and I hope will further extend the contributions of the federal government in the field of this country's social services.
As recently as two days ago I proposed to my provincial colleagues extended cost-sharing under hospital insurance and medical care, a cost-sharing extension which would have made life relatively easier for the provinces. Actually some provinces were eager to proceed immediately with the extension of those cost-sharing services. Other provinces prefer to wait until the first ministers' conference before making up their minds on this subject. Therefore it has been agreed that we shall wait until October 1 before reaching any conclusion on the subject.
We are not backing out of cost-sharing, not reducing the total volume of our contribution. We want to make certain that the health of Canadians keeps improving. But for this to happen we must allocate our resources to the most
Business of the House
efficient area and make sure that the taxpayers' dollars, the spending of which is our responsibility, are used for the best purpose.
Having heard representations in committee, and particularly the motion proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), I recognize that parliament ought to be given the opportunity to consider orders in council which the government might pass pursuant to the provisions of this bill. I therefore proposed motion No. 4, which is identical to a provision contained in Bill C-89. It provides that, at the request of 50 members of this House, an order in council must be debated for two days, after which there is to be a vote. If the vote is negative, the order in council shall become null and void. That provision, as I say, is identical to a similar provision contained in the bill on which the House voted earlier this afternoon. I hope it will carry, as it will give hon. members the opportunity to debate particular government decisions for a specified time.
Those are all the comments I wanted to make on the motions before the House. I thank hon. members for their attention.

subtopic: FLOODS-SOURIS RIVER AREA-POSSIBLE DECLARATION AS DISASTER AREA
FLOODS-SOURIS RIVER AREA-POSSIBLE DECLARATION AS DISASTER AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 12 I raised a question with respect to flooding on the Souris River. This is not a new problem. It is one that has been with the settlers in this area from time immemorial. However, it so happens that each year the problem is becoming increasingly worse. This year we have had intensive flooding which has involved major communities like Melita, Hartney, and the town of Souris itself, as well as thousands of acres of fertile farmland under flood waters and made useless for the current agriculture season, as well as extensive damage to wildlife.
The Souris River rises in Saskatchewan, winds into the United States, and then comes back into the province of Manitoba. For any action to deal with the growing problem of flooding, it will involve combined action on the part of at least five different governmental jurisdictions.
This year the city of Minot in the state of North Dakota was severely hit. It is estimated that damages will rise as high as $10 million. As a result the Governor of the state of North Dakota has asked the government of the United States to declare the area a national disaster.
Just to show how serious the flooding is this year, the Emergency Measures Organization calmly forecast that the flood would keep at a foot below the 1969 level. As actually happened, it peaked about ten feet above the flood level. Only effective work by the troops brought in on a very quick basis from the nearby Shilo Canadian Forces Base saved the water treatment plant in the town of Souris and also in the town of Melita. I would also like to note that students from the high school were released from school and did valiant work on the dikes as well.
The compensation is going to run into millions of dollars. As I have already indicated, the state of North Dakota will be backed by the resources of the United States. It appears that the Manitoba government is to bear the total cost of emergency compensation in the province of Manitoba through its Flood Assistance Board.
I raised the question on April 12 that the circumstances this year indicate that some permanent flood control measures must be taken on this waterway. I am sure all members are aware that over the past two or three years there has been constant discussion on the possible impact of the Garrison diversion that is being developed south of the border in terms of pollution of the Souris River and the

Red River, and the possible impact on Canadian territory as a result. The International Joint Commission is looking into this particular aspect of the problem of the Souris.
I strongly urge, as I did in my question to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand) the other day, that when he meets with the officials of the United States government, as he indicated he will be doing in the immediate future, he make strong representations that the terms of the IJC investigation be expanded to embrace the possibility and plans for permanent flood control on the Souris River.
There is a co-ordinating body that will involve the levels of government already operating in Canada. It was established on October 28, 1974, with the signing of an agreement by the governments of Canada, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. These governments jointly agreed to study the "complex and troublesome Souris River" and they established the study objective, which was as follows:
To carry out an assessment of the water and related resources of the Souris River Basin and of the demands being made and likely to be made on them-
Other objectives of the study were flood damage reduction-so this is specifically within the terms of reference- as well as water supply, water quality, agricultural matters, and water related resources. We have a body operating within Canada which has been gathering information now since 1974, so I suggest that Canada is in a very excellent position to make strong recommendations to the government of the United States in this respect.
I would also point out that there is an excellent precedent for the action on the part of intergovernmental bodies, at least on the Canadian level. In 1950 the city of Winnipeg was almost totally inundated by a disastrous flood. Following that flood, studies were undertaken which indicated that the only solution was permanent flood control. In the early 1960's-I will not mention the government that was in power at the time but it was a very effective government-the federal government started a program that we hoped would continue, but there has been no further development in this regard. Nevertheless the precedent was so effectively established with control of the Assiniboine River, the Shellmouth dam, the Portage diversion, and the Winnipeg floodway, that there is no longer any threat of flooding in the city of Winnipeg from the Assiniboine and Red Rivers.
I hope the minister will seize the initiative in meetings with United States officials. In light of the reaction of the Governor of the state of North Dakota, who has had to cope with a flood of the Souris River of unusual magnitude, the minister can be assured of the utmost co-operation from that level of government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government at this time has not received any request from the province of Manitoba for cost sharing assistance in respect to spring flooding along the Souris and Assiniboine River systems. I am advised, however, that the province will be establishing a flood damage compensation and restoration program to deal with the aftermath of the flood and that the costs of the program could be substantial. It is therefore likely that the province will be seeking federal finan-
April 29, 1976

cial assistance. The hon. member may rest assured that, when it is received, Manitoba's request will be given every consideration.
As the hon. member is aware, it has been long standing practice of the federal government to assist the provinces financially in the event that the cost of disasters exceed an amount that the provinces could reasonably be expected to bear on their own. Although the province of Manitoba is thoroughly familiar with the terms and conditions of the federal disaster assistance program, it might be useful for the members present if I briefly reviewed the chief aspects of the program.
As I have already noted, the federal policy has been deliberately designed to deal only with the larger, more costly disasters. This is clearly reflected in the cost sharing formula which establishes a minimum cost sharing threshold of $1 per capita of provincial population. No federal financial assistance is given until the costs incurred by a province exceed this minimum threshold. However, as costs rise above this level they are shared with the federal government on a progressive basis. Under the formula, which has been in effect since 1970, the amount of the federal contribution payable to a province is determined as follows: 0 per cent of the first $1 per capita of provincial expenditure, 50 per cent of the next $2 per capita of provincial expenditure, 75 per cent of the next $2 per capita of provincial expenditure, and 90 per cent of provincial expenditures in excess of $5 per capita.
In addition to the formula, there is a set of administrative guidelines which define the types of disaster related expenditures incurred by a province which are eligible for cost sharing assistance. Generally speaking, eligible expenditures are those made to restore the essential personal property of private citizens, farmsteads, and small businesses to habitable or workable condition, and to restore public works to their pre-flood condition. This also includes the costs of coping with the immediate situation such as building dikes and providing emergency accommodation. On the other hand, insurable losses, crop losses, and damages sustained by larger commercial enterprises are not eligible for cost-sharing assistance with the federal government.
As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) is aware, the Canadian forces personnel based in Shilo, Portage, and Winnipeg have been heavily involved this spring in combating the flood threat, particularly in the towns of Souris and Wawanesa. This is a clear indication of the federal government's concern over the emergency situation in Manitoba and of the federal government's willingness to assist Canadian citizens in this area of provincial and municipal jurisdiction.

TRANSPORT-SUGGESTION NEW POLICY BE DEVELOPED BEFORE ELIMINATION OF RAIL SUBSIDIES ON FLOUR AND GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say I can appreciate the dilemma you are facing at this hour of the night.
Over the Easter weekend I had the privilege of marching down two sheds in Halifax that were the length of about nine football fields, I think. They would have docked the Queen Elizabeth and the Queen Mary end to end without giving them a chance to rub bow to stern. Imagine that! Loaded there as high as an elephant can reach, and much higher than I can reach, and I am not exactly small, were bags of flour. This was the extent, as I saw it, of the flour trade that goes out through the Port of Halifax. It is a large trade. As a matter of fact I was rather surprised, and my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) can back me up, to find that it was larger than either one of us had thought was the case.
In any event, I am here tonight with a file of speeches that is about four inches thick which I have made on the late, late show. I think that in itself has to be a record. I do not think anyone has made more speeches on the late show on any one single subject, with the possible exception of the merry member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) who tangled some years ago with a former Postmaster General, Mr. Kierans. They used to joust here I think about once a week, if not twice a week on occasion.
In any event, I have pursued this with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Even the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) has not escaped my eagle eye on this subject.
I gather that our dear friend, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), is going to reply as best he can to this continuous thunder I am bringing up. I am not going to burden the House at this late hour with a lot of figures. What I am trying to burden the House with is a couple of arguments.
The first argument I hope I will be able to make successfully, and I will be backed up by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski), and others who are going to join this debate later on if it gets to that, is that I am going to prove brilliantly, conclusively, and beyond a reasonable doubt that the transportation subsidy in Canada is not in respect of Crowsnest Pass rates or maritime freight rates, but in respect of the St. Lawrence Seaway.
In looking around I see there are five people present, plus the ubiquitous member from the Canadian Press; one person on that side, one person by the clock, and our protective staff so I am protected from God knows what, and yourself, Mr. Speaker. This number will be increased because before this debate is over, and I guarantee this if not threaten it, people are going to know that the fattest subsidies in transportation in Canada are not paid to westerners or maritimers but to those who live along the St. Lawrence system from Quebec City to Thunder Bay.

That having been said I wish to mention one further point the Minister of Transport deliberately has dragged into this debate late in the day. After I believe the fourth occasion on which I raised this matter in the Chamber the minister said would it not be nice if we had a unit train from western Canada to Halifax. The fact is that the roadbed is not strong enough to handle it now. I say that one should not throw out an old policy until one has tried the new policy.
My view is that the Minister of Transport is not justified in attempting to bring in the red herring of the unit train between western Canada and Halifax, which will not work unless a great deal of money is spent on it. He is not justified in throwing out a policy which now works. This is a matter which affects every eastern port. It affects the port of Halifax, the port of Saint John, the port of Montreal, and it affects the St. Lawrence River, Toronto itself, Thunder Bay, Port Colborne, and all the grain growers, at least in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Until the minister does something about this I, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, the hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Vegreville, and the Lord knows how many other members from Ontario and Montreal will be involved in this. There will be a fight. That is the reason why I am standing up tonight.

subtopic: FINANCE-ALLEGED IMPORTATION OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS FROM UNITED STATES AT BELOW COST OF PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
FINANCE-ALLEGED IMPORTATION OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS FROM UNITED STATES AT BELOW COST OF PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the turn of the century a great American orator made the comment, prophetically I believe, that if we destroy the farm it will not be long before the grass grows in the streets of every city of the country. But if the cities should be destroyed, they will grow again so long as we preserve the farms. Nobody wants to see either cities or farms destroyed, but I am concerned that in Canada we are not looking after the farmers, and in the future we will pay dearly for that.
Farmers are facing problems from every direction. Tonight I am speaking specifically about farmers in my riding of Surrey-White Rock who are facing distress, partly because of flooding which results from the urbanization of the area next door to the farms, which creates an increased run-off problem, flooding the flat lands where the best farmland is. Also they are facing the problem of high labour costs, and the most important subject of my comments tonight is the matter of imports that are competing, I believe unfairly, with the production of farmers in Surrey and, as a matter of fact, in the whole of Canada.
On April 12 I raised the matter in the House, first addressing myself to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I spoke about the fact that at the time when fresh vegetables are ready for the market in the lower mainland of British Columbia fresh vegetables also happen to come in from the United States. It so happens that the American farmers can raise three or four crops a year, and with that kind of production it is easy for them to compete with the Canadian farmers and to maintain a high price all year long, and especially at the time when Canadian farmer's products are coming on the market when they can lower their price and still sell their product at above the cost for them. So they are not really technically guilty of dumping, but it is a matter of distress to Canadian farmers who cannot compete with that kind of import.
At the same time I mentioned to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) the fact that the processor of Canadian farm goods in Canada is facing competition from what is called distress selling of the product coming in from the U.S. As I understand it, distress selling is not really dumping, but it is providing again the kind of competition that is unfair to Canadian farmers.
For example, the frozen foods coming in from the U.S. are a commodity which can be preserved and does not have to be sold at any specific time. The large producer and the
April 29, 1976

large processor in the United States, with the volume they have, can easily bring that product to Canada and thus create unfair competition which is destroying Canadian farms. The U.S. can dominate in that way.
We had ten vegetables coming in from Taiwan at 20 per cent to 40 per cent below the market price of the Canadian product. We have mushrooms coming in from Korea and Taiwan. Recently Taiwan has been exporting frozen mushrooms. Until recently the mushroom farmers in Canada were selling mainly on the fresh market, and what they could not sell on the fresh market they froze and then sold. But now they are facing competition from these imports from Taiwan. You cannot blame farmers in Taiwan or the exporters, but we have to look after the producer in Canada.
What distresses me about this is that the consumer is caught in a bind. We cannot blame the consumer for that, but what will happen in the long run when smaller farmers are driven out of business and cannot compete any more? It will not be long until all we will have will be consolidated farms which will be similar to a monopoly and once that monopoly has been established, the consumer will get it in the neck anyway. It is only a matter of time.
All we need to do is to have a floating tariff which the Minister of Agriculture says is very simple. He is negotiating all the time but he does not seem to get around to providing that protective tarrif for our farmers in time so that our product is protected. All we need to do is raise that tariff in time so that the Canadian product finds shelter from the cheaper import from the United States. The Americans do that. They look after their own.
We have a reciprocal trade agreement with the United States, and there is supposed to be something like a 35 per cent or 37 per cent tariff on potatoes, for example. The Americans reciprocate, but they are shrewd enough and sharp enough to impose a quota on that part of the reciprocal trade agreement, and beyond that they impose a 75 per cent tariff. The quota is low enough so that it does not even pay Canadians to export, so we are defeated before we begin.
All I am asking of the Minister of Finance is that he consider the Canadian farmer and the distress under which he is operating and the kind of competition he is facing, and protect him so that in the years to come we will
Adjournment Debate
have production in our country and consumers will be protected in the long run. When a monopoly is established the consumer will be grabbed by the throat, and we will be paying, and paying in a way we cannot afford. All we are asking of the minister is that he look into the future so that our farmers will be protected, and in the long run our consumers will also be protected.

subtopic: FINANCE-ALLEGED IMPORTATION OF AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS FROM UNITED STATES AT BELOW COST OF PRODUCTION-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) raised several interesting points. One I do not intend to comment on is the flooding he referred to because on the previous flooding issue I think I was washed out to sea.
I will try to be very specific with regard to the question of April 12 which the hon. member raised as to tariffs. I wish to advise that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) wrote to the president of Royal City Foods Limited on March 25. In his letter the minister pointed out that the Tariff Board is currently reviewing the tariffs on fresh and processed fruits and vegetables. He also made reference to the procedures already available under the Antidumping Act to deal with any imports Royal City Foods Limited believes are being dumped on the Canadian market.
I might add that in response to representations the minister later received from the Canadian Food Processors' Association, senior officials of the Department of Finance and of other interested departments met with representatives of that association to discuss the difficulties which have been encountered recently in certain segments of the processed fruits and vegetables industry in Canada. Representatives of the industry have undertaken to provide certain additional information concerning the impact of import competition on their operations which will assist the government in reaching a decision on the request of the industry for additional protection against imports.
I hope this information will satisfy the hon. member. His concern is shared by many hon. members of this House.
